newsitem.title: USA: North Dakota floods test dikes, residents.
newsitem.headline: North Dakota floods test dikes, residents.

text.p: Hundreds of volunteers worked feverishly on Wednesday to build backup dikes in Fargo as the rushing Red River rose ever higher, to its highest water mark this century, more than 20 feet (6 metres) over flood stage.

"We just don't want to let up," said Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness. "The worst may yet be coming for all we know. The problem is nobody does know ... We don't know how long those sandbag dikes are going to hold up," he said.

As he spoke to reporters, workers who had been on duty through the night were building a 6-foot-(2 metre)-long secondary earthen dike running more than four blocks through downtown in the middle of Third Street near City Hall.
A second dike was being built in a northeast side neighbourhood where officials fear hundreds of homes could be flooded if the permanent levee there fails.

Upstream on the Red River at Breckenridge, Minnesota, nearly 500 people had been forced from their homes and the advancing river threatened still more. Among those driven out were residents of a senior citizens complex who left in Coast Guard boats and National Guard trucks.
Water in parts of the southern section of Breckenridge was 12 feet (3.6 metres) deep.

In Fargo at midday the Red had risen to nearly 39 feet (12 metres) -- more than 20 feet (6 metres) over flood stage and the highest since a massive 1897 flood. Dennis Walaker, operations director for Fargo's Public Works department, said he did not expect the river to rise much beyond 39 feet.

"We are going to be in harm's way at least through the weekend before we see any significant drop," he said. One good piece of news was that the river was flowing very fast -- meaning that the valley was now draining rapidly.

Farther north at Grand Forks, where the highest water is expected early next week, the North Dakota Highway Patrol closed a section of Interstate 39, the area's main north-south artery into Canada. A second section of the same road in the Fargo area has been closed since last week.
The Red, gorged with runoff from a record winter snowfall in the northern plains, was still rising but at a slower pace than on Tuesday.
North Dakota State University closed on Wednesday to allow students, faculty and staff to join the emergency efforts.
Flooding has forced the evacuation of many small cities and rural areas along the Red and its tributaries which flow northward into Canada.

In Grand Forks the Red was at 47.5 feet (14.5 metres) on Wednesday and city officials had plans to evacuate low-lying areas when the river reaches its expected 50-foot (15.24 metre) crest, Byron Sieber, spokesman for the city's Emergency Operations Centre, said.

Two of three bridges connecting the city to East Grand Forks, Minnesota, have been closed and the third was threatened. Sieber said every effort will be made to keep open the third bridge, which should withstand the anticipated river level.
"We would be doing the diking at the landings on each end of the bridge," he said.

The United States Coast Guard conducted helicopter surveys north of Fargo on Tuesday but no rescues of flood-stranded residents were necessary, Chief Warrant Officer Randy Caverly at the Coast Guard's Fargo office said.
Earlier this week, residents, their willpower drained by nearly a week of being surrounded by high water, appealed to the Coast Guard and emergency crews for rescue.
